speechtext: Hon. E. N. RHODES (Minister of Finance) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 114 relating to the application of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, 1934, in the province of British Columbia.
Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the objects sought to be attained in the passing of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act are well known to the house. In a word the main object was to try to compose the debt structure of a farmer to the point where he could meet his obligations and remain upon the land as a producer.
I think it is fair to say that the act has met with a remarkably favourable reception throughout the country. I desire to pay tribute to the provincial governments for their cordial cooperation, in the main, with the Department of Finance in endeavouring to administer the act. Every province, with the exception of British Columbia-and I will refer to that province in a moment-has cooperated not only to the point of facilitating the operation of the act in every way through contact with its several officials but has made contributions in the way of reductions in fees, and no province has taken any exception to the general terms of the act in its application to provincial obligations. That statement is true as far as the province of British Columbia is concerned from the inception of the act in November until the month of May. During the month of May the board of review sat on a case concerning one Copeland, and it is fair to assume that the province did not object to the jurisdiction of the board because it was represented there by the attorney general. In the Copeland case the board of review made the following finding with regard to the claim of the province of British Columbia for arrears of taxes upon the land:
-that all interest due thereon, with penalties be written off



Fanners' Creditors Act-Mr. Mackenzie
I interpret that to mean that the decision was that the interest upon arrears of taxes should be written off.
-and that the amount payable be allowed and fixed at the sum of $1,408.03 (which is inclusive of the taxes assessed and payable in 1935); and that the said sum shall be payable in three equal annual instalments of $469.34, each, without interest, on the 31st day of October in the years 1936, 1937 and 1938 respectively; and the board directs that no tax enforcement proceeding shall be taken against the debtor in respect of these payments until after October 31, 1939,	The
debtor shall pay all current taxes payable to the province in the year 1936 and subsequent years until and including the year 1940, regularly and in accordance with the provisions of the statute in that behalf.
In May it was announced by the attorney general of that province that the province proposed to challenge the legality of the act.
The premier of the province said that it created an invasion of provincial rights, and he proposed to fight- it all along the line. As a result of the finding in the case I have just indicated the province appeared before the court and asked' for a declaration-
1.	(a) That the defendants purporting to act as a "Board of review for the province of British Columbia" under the provisions of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. being chapter 53 of the statutes of Canada. 1934, and amending acts and the rules and regulations passed thereunder, are acting without lawful authority, as the said act is ultra vires the parliament of Canada.
(b) Alternatively, that the board of review is acting without lawful authority in assuming jurisdiction under the said act to formulate proposals and to make directions by virtue of which contracts and taxation powers and rights of the crown in the right of the province of British Columbia in relation to farmer debtors are in whole or in part abrogated and set aside.
2.	The plaintiff further claims an injunction to restrain the defendants from purporting to formulate proposals or to give directions or to make orders involving contracts by the crown n11 *"?[DOT] r'sht _ of the province of British Columbia and its farmer debtors in relation to amounts owing under such contracts to the said province and' in relation to moneys due or to become due from farmer debtors to the crown in the right of the said province in respect of any form of taxes, fees, rates or duties.
An interim restraining order was granted on June 15, the motion to continue the injunction being returnable on June 27.
In coming to its decision to introduce this bill the government has had in mind the fact that since the inception of the act there have been, up to the end of May, 57.610 interviews, 10,942 proposals, and 4,602 settlements. These are formal settlements effected by the receivers. In addition there have been 1,250 settlements effected as a result 
of decisions of boards of review. Of that number only 58 occurred in the province of British Columbia as a result of settlements effected by the receivers and I believe only six or seven as a result of decisions by boards of review.
In an interview reported in the press of to-day, or possibly yesterday, the premier of British Columbia said that he was quite content that the act should be applicable so long as it does not apply to the province of British Columbia. In other words, he is quite content that contributions shall be made by loan companies, by trust companies, by banks, by insurance companies and by private debtors, but the province itself should be immune. It will stand on the letter of the law and it will exact its pound of flesh.
It is not for me to quarrel with the decision of the province. It is within the rights of the provincial government to take the attitude it may desire to take, but in making my statement I am stating the blunt facts. There are two things to be said. One is that we have the right to assume that the government of British Columbia speaks for the province of British Columbia, and by its attitude it has said, "We do not wish this act applicable to the province of British Columbia." But the second and more important consideration is this. While we are advised by the Department of Justice that this law is intra vires of this parliament, what a court of law might do is another matter. And inasmuch as the law has been accepted as applicable to the other eight provinces of Canada I submit that we would be derelict in our duties if we were to imperil its existence and the benefits which flow from its operation in the other eight provinces if we allowed the act to continue in British Columbia, with the results which might flow from the action which has been taken in the courts by that province. In these circumstances we have felt that we have no alternative but that of introducing this measure.

Mr. Speaker, I regret very much that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) has departed from the customary courtesies extended on the occasion of the first reading of a bill, and has sought to make a detailed explanation which would have been more proper on second reading. I would say to the minister that he has raised some very controversial arguments. I am not here to defend or to protest against action which may be taken by the provincial government of the province of British Columbia. I am personally in favour, and have so expressed myself

Canada-Poland Trade Treaty
repeatedly, of the provisions of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act in the province of British Columbia. My right hon. friend, the leader of the opposition, very definitely expressed himself as being in favour of the provisions of the bill when it was discussed in the house.
I must protest most emphatically however against the Minister of Finance, at this time and at this stage of debate, namely, upon the introduction of a bill which we have not yet seen, to the consideration of this house, imputing motives to any provincial government, whether it be Liberal or Conservative, I do not care which. I am certainly disposed to object to this bill; I may say frankly to the minister that I am in favour of the application of the provisions of the act to the province of British Columbia. I have spoken in favour of it, and so has the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid), upon many occasions in British Columbia. For these reasons I say it is entirely unbecoming in the minister, when he seeks leave of the house to introduce the bill, to impute motives when the full facts are not in possession of the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think it is due to me that I be given the opportunity to say that if the bon. member would do me the courtesy of reading what I have said he could not take exception to a single statement I have made when introducing the bill. In doing more than stating in simple terms what the bill sought to do I was merely being courteous to the house at this stage so that hon. members might be fully aware of the motives which have caused the government to introduce the bill. I must say however that I did not impute any motives to the province of British Columbia. I confined my observations entirely to a statement of facts, and only a limited number of those facts at that, from official documents. I believe when the hon. member reads what I have said he will realize that the last thing I attempted to do or had in mind, or that the government had in mind, was to show any partisanship, because I was at pains to pay tribute to the other provinces in Canada, without regard to their political affiliations, for having cooperated so loyally with the federal government in the administration of the act. After all, the chief motive is to serve the agricultural population of Canada, and I believe we may forget the political phase of it.
I wish you had.

That is all you are thinking about.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

DISABLED PENSIONERS AT WINNIPEG On the orders of the day:

Mr. Speaker just before this sitting

commenced I had a telegram from Winnipeg concerning which I telephoned my hon. friend the Minister of Pensions and National Health and I rise now to make inquiry from him with regard to the situation which apparently has developed in Winnipeg among the disabled pensioners there. Apparently the complaint is that the Department of Pensions and National Health is not complying with a regulation which these men assert has been made whereby a five-dollar allowance was to be exempted from any deduction which is to be made in connection with the relief grant. There are about 400 pensioners now camped in the grounds of Deer Lodge hospital and they threaten to stay there until the regulations are complied with. Can the minister make a statement in regard to this matter?

speakeroldname: Hon. D. M. SUTHERLAND (Minister of Pensions and National Health):
speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the general principle that is applied in the granting of relief is that the department supplements the amount that is given to small pensioners to bring it up to the amount that is granted by the muncipalities to civilians on relief.
Some little time ago the municipal council of Winnipeg decided to allow an exemption of S5 to imperial pensioners who had come to this country since 1924. When they were estimating the amount of relief which a man might receive they said, "We will not count $5 of your pension as income." The result was that such an imperial pensioner would receive $5 more in relief. This organization sent several telegrams to the department claiming that they should also have $5 more in relief but I could not see that they were entitled to this. These exemptions were not made in connection with civilian relief and these men were telegraphed to to the effect that no decision would be given at the time as the Hyndman commission had made several recommendations with regard to relief which were under consideration. In spite of that reply a certain number went to the hospital at Deer Lodge and intimated that they intended to stay until their demands were granted. I believe about forty spent last night on the grounds under canvas.
Is it the intention of the department to give this matter further consideration or does the department consider it at an end?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
The department is
always willing to consider anything.

The house resumed from Friday, June 14, consideration in committee of Bill No. 85, to amend the Companies Act, 1934-Mr. Cahan- Mr. Smith (Cumberland) in the chair.
Section 1 agreed to.
On section 2-Incorporation only for objects and powers to 'be actively pursued.
Does the minister think that this section makes any real alteration in the act as it is at the present time?

I believe the hon. gentleman could give an opinion on that just as well as I. This section was drafted to carry out the recommendations of the commission and I think it does so. In actual practice I do not think it will make very much difference with a great many companies as in any case they would operate entirely within this section. This section will restrict the activities of a oompany to the purposes and objects stated in the application for letters patent and in the letters patent as granted.

In making an application for letters patent is it not usual to set out all the objects which the company believes they will want to make use of? The powers granted are usually very broad and as I see it this section would restrict those powers.

As far as my memory goes, years ago when a company applied for letters patent they proposed very broad powers but that has not been the practice in recent years. In recent years the companies have limited their applications to certain specific objects, and then there are other implied powers incidental thereto. The real difference of opinion which arises in the courts is brought about by another issue. A company may be restricted to its objects and powers as expressed in its charter, but those dealing with the company may rely to a certain extent upon its having the particular powers which it holds itself out to have. In connection with the Obligations of a company to its creditors and to those who have made contracts with it, there is a tendency in the court decisions to assume that the company as a company is responsible for the holding out by its officers of the possession of certain powers. I think the provisions of this section are very strict and that they will carry out the purposes which the commission had in mind when making the report it did with regard to this particular matter.

Am I correct in assuming that it is the minister's opinion that this section will have the effect of curtailing the operations of a company and preventing it from carrying on any business which may be conducive to the main object for which it is incorporated?

I do not think the hon. member should assume that at all. That is a very
Companies Act Amendment

broad issue and I certainly cannot give my adherence to any such suggestion. The powers which are conducive to the interests of a company offer a much wider field than those which are merely incidental.

The provision is that if a company carries on business contrary to or exceeds the powers it shall be liable to be wound up as if it had become insolvent. I point out that the Winding-up Act expressly provides that a company shall be liable to be wound up in any event in which, according to the Companies Act, it is to be dissolved; so that there is no need! to provide that a company shall be wound up as if it were insolvent. All that is necessary-and it makes the procedure much more simple-is to provide that such companies shall be liable to be dissolved if they do the things enumerated, and the Winding-up Act comes in and declares that this is one of the cases in which the company may be wound up. I wonder what the draftsman had in mind when he proposed to have the company wound up as if it were insolvent. In that event a great many things would have to be done with .regard to the creditors, procedure and matters of that sort which might be avoided if this section simply provided that in the events mentioned the company is liable to be dissolved!

The drafting is not mine
the section was drafted by the officials of the Department of Justice. My own personal .opinion concurs largely in the suggestion of my hon. friend, that if a company is liable to be dissolved it is liable to be dissolved under the provisions of the Winding-up Act, and under that act any company which is insolvent may be wound up. I suppose the draftsman regarded this as being an assertion in more particular language of the *very position which the hon. gentleman has taken. If the hon. gentleman wishes to move such an amendment I do not think there need be much controversy.

I have not got it written out, but my motion would be that the words "wound up" in line 30 be struck out and the words, in lines 31 and 32 "as if it had become insolvent" be also struck out and the word "dissolved" be inserted after the words "to be" in line 30, so that the provision would read:
such company shall be liable to be dissolved under the provisions of the Winding-up Act, and the attorney general of Canada may, upon receipt of a certificate of the Secretary of State setting forth his opinion as in this section provided, apply to a court of competent jurisdiction for an order that the company be wound up.
In the thirtieth line the hon. member would strike out the words "wound up" and insert in lieu thereof the word "dissolved."
That is right.
And in lines 31 and 32 the words "as if it. had become insolvent" would be struck out and the rest of the section would remain the same.
Yes.

I believe it has the same
effect.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
Section 3 agreed to.
On section 4-Shares to be allotted for consideration fixed by board of directors.

Attention was drawn
on Friday last to the continuance of no par shares and distributable surplus. I am assuming that the minister has not changed his mind in that regard. I will not press the point brought to his attention last year and this year again.

In all my long experience I have always found that fixing the par values at $100 or a proportion thereof enabled one to carry out the purposes of the company quite fully. That is my own experience with respect to those matters which have been brought before me in my professional capacity. I am prepared to lay on the table of the house a long list of scores of companies, among the most active in our commercial and industrial life, which have no par value shares and which are now operating. Whatever parliament may do in future revisions, at the present time to abolish no par value shares would be to compel scores of these companies to reconstruct at a time of great distress and difficulty, and I do not think the time is opportune.
Mr. BOTHWEiLL: Might it not be well to stop other incorporations in the future from issuing no par shares, even if the old companies were left?

Another parliament might be in a clearer frame of mind to consider that question. In all cases that have come before me, and there have been many in the last five years, I have not seen one in which no par value shares were used as a means of stock-watering. Under the system of accounting we now have, every statement of a company must show clearly the value of

Companies Act Amendment
these nio par value shares, and this improved accounting system is excluding water where water was brought iu under previous conditions of organization. No doubt from time to time the Companies Act must be revised to meet real difficulties, to overcome real objections and- to abolish evils as they creep up, but at the present time these companies are all objecting to the possibility of their organization being crippled and their effective recovery being postponed for a considerable time.
Was not that one of the promises in the reform program outlined in the radio addresses?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It certainly was; and what is more, I said that if the price spreads commission recommended the abolition of no par shares I would vote for it. I will vote for it to-day if there is a motion to that effect.
It is true as well that the price spreads commission in its wisdom did not recommend it. .
We were not given to understand in the radio speeches that the Prime Minister would be governed by what the price spreads commission might recommend.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I referred to that also.
No.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I beg your pardon,

In January the addresses were to the effect that so and so would be done, and among other things it was indicated that no par value shares would be done away with. May I ask the Secretary of State what he thinks personally about it. Was he of the opinion that they should be abolished?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I also said that the
recommendations of the price spreads commission would be given effect to. I assumed, as I said the other day, that they would be within the law, and to the extent that we are advised they are we have endeavoured to give effect to them. The commission put no par value shares in the alternative. Had they suggested, as 1 understood the views of many of the commission were, that they should be abolished, certainly it would have been so found.
The only answer is that the government has not carried out the alternative.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Oh yes.
The commission recommended that no par value shares be abolished or that there be no distributable surplus. The government has not carried out that recommendation.
That is quite different. I have no wish to discuss such a very fine point as that, but under this bill there could be no distributable surplus created out of capital.
That is what I mean.
By this bill there can be none.

I do not think that is the effect of the bill. That is only as it applies to capital paid in before the passing of this legislation. It is possible under this legislation for part of the capital to be carried to distributable surplus.

No. I think I can assure my hon. friend that the process, which has been carried on whereby from time to time directors, with the approval of a majority of the shareholders-I think it is a three-quarter majority-can set aside as distributable surplus that which has been received as capital, is abolished.

Section 2 commencing at line 15 on page 2 of the bill reads:
And in fixing the amount of such consideration, the board, subject to the provisions of this part, may provide in the contract of subscription for such shares that the consideration received therefor shall be deemed to be capital, excepting a part, if any, not exceeding twenty-five per centum thereon, which shall be set aside as distributable surplus.

It is not then received as capital at all. Under this bill if it becomes law, it will be impossible for a company to set aside as distributable surplus anything which it has received as capital; but in the initial subscription it may make a contract with its subscriber as to what part of the consideration shall apply to capital, and that a certain percentage may apply as distributable surplus, not necessarily for dividends but for carrying on the company without impairment of its capital, because this percentage is no longer capital. I think this bill under the circumstances goes very far in the way of reform. We have abolished this practice which has been going on with regard to setting aside from time to time a certain portion of the capital of the company as distributable surplus.
In early times I believe there were certain fixed assets that were set aside as distribut-
Companies Act Amendment

able surplus, but under the regulations which have prevailed in the department for a number of years now, nothing can be set aside as distributable surplus except it be a portion of the liquid, realizable assets. I think we have gone a long way in reform by providing that if a shareholder wishes to put up, in addition to his subscription to capital, a certain sum as distributable surplus to ensure the stability of the company, we will not prohibit him. I douibt if we could. I think that, if I am a shareholder of a company, it would be very difficult to prohibit me from making a contribution to its treasury to enable it to carry on whether the company called that contribution distributable surplus or anything else. I think the hon. gentleman will find we are going a very long way to meet the views of the commission.

Section agreed to.
On section-Consideration for any shares allotted must be adequate.

In reading over this clause,
1	think the word "less" in line 36 on page
2	should be "more." How it got in in that form I do not know. I think the clause should read:
In no case shall any shares, whether common or preferred, or whether with or without nominal or par value, be issued and allotted as fully or partly paid up for more than what may justly be deemed to be-
I fancy in an early draft, that was drafted in another way and the word "less" was retained inadvertently. I suggest that the change I have indicated should be made.
I think the word should be "less."

I cannot agree with the minister. The clause reads:
In no case shall any shares, whether common or preferred, or whether with or without nominal or par value, be issued and allotted as fully or partly paid up for less than what may justly be deemed in all the circumstances of the case adequate consideration therefor.
As it reads now, it means that the company is not able to issue shares unless they have been paid for. According to my interpretation the word should be "less" instead of "more."
Allow me to read the clause again because it was an hon. member who drew my attention to it. Yes, I think the hon. member is right; I was mistaken.

There is just one other question in connection with the section. It reads:
[Mr Cahan.]
For less than what may justly be deemed in all the circumstances of the case adequate consideration therefor in cash, property or services.
Then in section 96B, under section 15 of the bill at page 9 these words are used:
It shall not be lawful for the directors or promoters of a company to authorize the issue and allotment of any shares of the capital stock of the company as fully paid up unless the company receives, or is to receive what may justly be deemed, in all the circumstances of the case, adequate consideration therefor in cash, property or services.
Just taking those two sections together, I am wondering whether, under section 5 when reference is made to adequate consideration in services, that may be services to be rendered as referred to in the new section 96B, because it seems to me that section 96B will have to be changed, as under the section as I read it no company is able to issue shares for services to be rendered in futurity.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Why not add a word
to make it clear that that is for something past and not in the future?
Section 5 may be clear so far as it is concerned if we alter section 96B when we come to it, but I wanted to bring the matter to the attention of the minister now.

In regard to the matter
to which I referred before, simply to show that I was speaking inadvertently, I was sent through a member of the house a short memorandum from the Dominion Association of Chartered Accountants as follows:
If the proposed section (9) of this act is to remain, should not the word "less" in the third line read "more"?
As this came from such an important body, I thought there could not possibly be a mistake, but the suggestion that any change should be made has now been entirely withdrawn.

My difficulty with this
section is what I conceive to be its absolute unworkability and the uncertainty which it is going to create among people who happen to buy shares. I may be wrong about this, but the effect of this section appears to be this. It means that if a company is incorporated under the Dominion Companies Act, and for instance I am an officer of it, I agree to serve the company for $100 a month plus ten shares, doing that because I know the company is in hard circumstances and the directors think it is a good thing to take me on because it means I have an interest in the progress of the company; in other words,

Companies Act Amendment
if I make a success of the company my shares will be worth something. I sell my shares to someone else. Five years afterwards, the company gets into financial difficulties and is wound uip. Mr. X, the man to whom I sold the shares, is put on the list of contributories of the company. He asks why? He is told that it is because of the fact that as regards those shares, although issued fully paid up, the consideration, that is Ralston's services, did not represent adequate consideration for the shares. He is told "you are liable to pay the difference between the real value of Ralston's services and the par value of the shares." I think that is the effect of this section. I think it means that no man can buy the shares of a dominion company without the fear that at some later date a liquidator may put him on the list of contributors and say to the judge, "We want you to project your mind back to the time these shares were issued, to find out if in all the circumstances adequate consideration therefor was given in cash, property or services."
I take that illustration about salary because X happen to know of a case which is all finished with now, so I can speak of it quite freely. It was the subject of considerable discussion in another city. A managing director was given certain shares in addition to his salary; he cut his salary about in two and took shares in place of part of it. That man is getting those shares to-day. This act does not apply to him, so there can be no trouble about it, but if that had happened after this act came into force it w-ould seem that a person who might buy shares from him would face the possibility of some liquidator or creditor coming in and saying that man's services were not worth the number of shares given to him, and the holder of the shares might be required to pay the balance.
That is the situation from the point of view of the shareholder. The point of view of the adviser is just the reverse. Somebody is asked to advise whether these shares were fully paid up. They are marked paid up on their face, but that is not enough. Were they actually issued for less than what -might justly be deemed, "in all the circumstances of the case, adequate consideration therefor in cash, property or services." I do not know of any legal or business adviser who can forecast the mind of a judge having to decide ten years hence what the circumstances were at the time the shares were issued. On that ground, therefore, it seems to me that the section is unworkable and dangerous. I am fully in accord with the idea of not having shares issued for fictitious considerations. As the Secretary of State knows, under the English act there was a provision .whereby, if shares are issued for anything else than cash, the agreement must be filed showing exactly what was the consideration for those shares, so that anyone buying shares may know that the company did not receive cash for them but something in place of cash.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The prospectus will
show that.

Quite right. Under the amendments of last year there was required to be stated in the prospectus itself what was the consideration for the shares. That is, you cannot just say so many dollars; you must specify the property or the thing for which the shares were issued.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Services or contemplated services.

Or, in my case, service for so -many years as a portion of the salary, So the shareholder knows exactly the sort of consideration that was given and the extent of that consideration, and it is up to him to put a value on those services and decide whether or not they represented adequate consideration. But it seems to me to impose on what might be innocent holders, the liability of facing a law-suit to decide the question of the adequacy of the consideration at the time the shares were issued to the original allottee and it seems to me that is going to make it very inadvisable to incorporate under the Dominion Companies Act. It is not fair to the investor; I do not think it is fair to the business public, nor is it fair to the companies themselves, because in these times shares are issued for considerations other than cash, and perfectly good considerations too, which are just as valuable to the company as cash and for which people will accept shares in order that the cash position of the company may not be impaired. I suggest that the Secretary of State consider the matter further before this section passes in its present form.

The difficulty which the hon. gentleman has mentioned is obvious, but I think he forgets a decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in the early days, when I think Chief Justice Ritchie was presiding- and that decision never has been modified-in which it was held that if a company issues shares as fully paid and those shares are subsequently transferred from the first allottee to others, the third parties being without notice that the shares have not been fully paid when the certificate of the company shows that they are fully paid, are not liable either to the company or to a creditor. The
Companies Act Amendment

first purchaser of the shares, or perhaps it is better to say the first allottee of the shares, remains liable if the shares were issued for an inadequate consideration, but the third party does not. I have had very strong representations made, in regard to this section, that we should incorporate in it a provision of the English act under which the question of the inadequacy of the consideration, if raised, must be raised within a period of two years.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is by other than
the allotee?

I think this subject is worthy of clarification. We have section 15 of the bill which contains a proposed enactment of section 96B of the statute, and which deals with the subject of adequate consideration.

The new section 96B is a
penalty clause.

Yes, that is right. It imposes a penalty upon directors, among others, for doing what is forbidden by section 5. When I say it needs clarification I do not mean that I can clarify it to any great extent, but I am speaking in the presence of some able company lawyers, and perhaps they will be able to do so. I have had veiy little experience with the Dominion Companies Act-practically none. In the province of Nova Scotia where I have incorporated companies we have used the old English provision whereby an agreement is filed when property is transferred to the company and shares taken in consideration of the property.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The adequacy of consideration does not arise.

No. We never considered
that the adequacy of the consideration arose, at all. No matter how insignificant the property turned in, if we had an agreement covering it, that was sufficient.

Companies Act Amendment
I am afraid the hon. member is under a misapprehension as to the effect of the agreement in case the consideration is entirely inadequate.
In the light of some decisions which have been brought to my attention I think probably we did take too much for granted.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Nevertheless, it was quite a general practice.

Yes. We never had any
trouble incorporating companies in that way. I am not sure what the effect of the Dominion Companies Act would be. To begin with, there is no section in the Dominion Companies Act at the present time which states specifically that shares are issued subject to being paid for in full. The section which has the nearest application is section 45 of the act.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Is there not one respecting discounts?

Subsection 2 of section 45 states:
The liability of a shareholder in respect of any share held by him in the company in respect of which he is liable as a shareholder shall be limited (a) in the case of a share with nominal or par value to the amount unpaid thereon and (b) in the case of a share without nominal or par value to the amount of the consideration for which the share was issued by the company which is unpaid thereon.
Before the passing of that section last year there was a section in the previous act which appeared positively to impose a liability upon a shareholder to pay to the liquidator-
What was that section?
I am sorry I cannot give the number, but the section gave a creditor the right of action. It may have been merely procedure.

Quite so. The bon. member is dealing with the section which gave a creditor the right of personal action. If he will allow me to say so, we repealed that section, because it led to notorious inequalities. It was an old section adopted from early times from some New England statutes before we had a Winding-up Act or an Insolvency Act, and which1 enabled a creditor who had obtained a judgment against a company to proceed by scire facias against an individual shareholder. The result was that cases arose in Canada in which such proceedings were taken, and in which one creditor by proceeding independently got full compensation from shareholders who had not paid up, while
other creditors were left without any share in that consideration and without any possibility of recovering.
After the most careful discussion with the lawyers throughout the country we came to the conclusion that that process led to such gross inequalities that it should be repealed so that under the Winding-Up Act or under the Bankruptcy Act such assets as there were should be distributed equally. Now any creditor who has a claim of S500 against a company, which is not paid, may not recover individually, but he may take necessary proceedings for the winding up of a company and the equitable distribution of its assets, or he may proceed under the insolvency and achieve the same end. That is the reason that section was repealed.

Whatever the reason may be, the view has been expressed to me that the joint effect of section 45 and section 5 and that part of section 15 of the bill enacting section 96B is to do away with the rule that shares cannot be issued at a discount.

I differ from my hon. friend. I believe I have heard that suggestion elsewhere. Directors under our law as administered in all the English provinces, and as administered1 under the civil law in Quebec where they follow the English decisions, are deemed to be trustees, and are liable as such in respect of the administration of their office. I prefer that equity law which obtains in the English provinces and the civil law of Quebec as a means of enforcing the directors liability rather than any provisions in express terms such as the hon. member has suggested. There is no statutory provision under the English law, although since 1929 they have abolished this provision with regard to filing agreements disclosing the consideration received for the issues of shares. They preferred to abolish the filing of agreements under the English companies act and leave it to the courts of England to determine the trustees liabilities and obligations.
There may be some difference between the English companies which are incorporated by memorandum of association and these companies which are governed by the Bonanza case.

Not as to thie liability of
shareholders.

I d!o not know about that.
I do not put my views forward1 with very much confidence but that suggestion has been made. Let me try to make clear what
Companies Act Amendment

I have in my mind. If we pass these sections it is nowhere stated in the act that the shares have to be paid for in full. Section 45 says that the liability is limited to the amount unpaid on the shares, and this says that that consideration for the shares must be adequate.
Up to the par value.

If it stated that it would
probably do away with the difficulty, but the view has been advanced by persons who have some knowledge of company law that with these two sections, with section 45 merely imposing a negative limitation on the liability-not stating that they must be paid up in full, that they cannot be issued at a discount-and this section which says that the consideration for the shares must be adequate, that is the property, cash or service consideration, then by implication it is possible to issue shares at a discount under this bill as it is drafted, and that of course is undesirable. The sections have a different object altogether. It is to prevent the issuing of shares for less than adequate consideration. I suppose-the minister will correct me if I am wrong-that the desirable thing is that if the shares are shares having a nominal or par value everything should be done to assure that the allottee of the shares shall pay for them in full, whether he pays $100 cash for a SlOO-share or whether he gives $100 worth of property. That is the objective we are working towards. In the case of no par value shares the value placed on the books of the no par value shares shall be deemed to be the par value of the shares, and that- amount shall actually go into the company as the capital of the company. That I think is what is desired. I got in touch with Mr. Wegenast to find out what he had to say about this and he sent me this telegram which I am authorized' to read:
Ee proposed section 96B would undoubtedly make more difficult to bring home responsibility for stock watering. Present law requires consideration to be not merely adequate in all circumstances but to be equivalent of par value or issue price of stock although in some cases courts have shown reluctance to go behind honest decision of directors, see authorities collected page four ninety-four of my book. Simplest statement can make is that few if any cases I know that have succeeded against directors or promoters for stock watering would have succeeded under provisions like 96B.
I asked him how he would correct it in the act and I will send over to the minister his suggestions.
[Mr. Ilsley.l
I have read Mr. Wegenast's book and his citations of such cases. If the hon. gentleman has any amendment to suggest, let him suggest it. Let us get down to the heart of the thing.

I will finish what I have
to say. It is suggested under 96B which we have not yet reached-

Would my hon. friend allow me one moment to explain? Section 96iB is an entirely different section with an entirely different purport and intent from the section which we have under consideration, which is section 5. Section 5 deals with the person subscribing for shares paying adequate consideration therefor, but sections 96A, and 96B do not refer to subscribers for shares but impose penalities upon directors if they issue shares without adequate consideration. So the purposes in view are entirely different.
They are both directed to the same end.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: One is complementary to the other.
Yes.
One is an imposition of penalties on directors and the other has to do with the civil liability of the shareholders.

I realize that, but the adequacy referred to in these sections should be related to the par value or the issue price of the shares. But there is nothing to relate the adequacy of the consideration to the par value or the issue price of the shares.
What else could it relate to?

Well, whatever the court thinks under all the circumstances the shares are worth. That is what it says-"what may justly be deemed in all the circumstances of the case adequate consideration therefor." My hon. friend from Shelburne-Yarmouth suggests that section 45 does it but I am saying that perhaps it does not. It merely fixes an upper limit. It does not state there is a liability to pay up to the full value at all. There should be a section of the act reading like this:
Every shareholder shall, until the whole of the par value or the issue price as the case may be. of his shares shall have been paid up, be liable to pay to the company or to its liquidator or to the trustee in bankruptcy of its estate any amount unpaid on such shares.
That is a positive imposition of liability which does away with any implication such as I have suggested. I am going to suggest that section 96B, which is complementary, so

Companies Act Amendment
I do not think there can be any objection to discussing it now, be amended by adding this clause:
Nothing in this section shall have the effect of relieving any director or promoter from any liability to which he would have been subject at common law or the civil law before the passing of this section, or of preventing any suit or proceeding in respect of any such liability.
With these amendments I do not see any objection to these sections as they are drafted, but without them I suggest that they may not do their work.

If the hon. member will move his amendment and it is approved, it will be adopted of course, but where I do disagree entirely with the suggestion of the hon. gentleman and with the suggestion of Mr. Wegenast is this:	If we are to continue
the common law liability and the civil law liability, let us do so. It proves adequate in my experience. I have certainly in connection with one railway company made scores of shareholders pay up because the consideration paid was inadequate, as my hon. friend may read in the reports of the supreme court of Nova Scotia. There is no doubt as to what the liability is if you apply the law of trusts and trustees, which applies in all the English provinces, or if you have recourse to the civil law of the province of Quebec, but why render a statute complex by attaching to it the common law or the civil law. Let us have one liability or the other. This section 5 as drawn, in the opinion of the Department of Justice which drew it, covers the recommendation and the very terms of the recommendation of the commission. I suggest that the commission of which my hon. friend was a member in making that recommendation should have studied the matter more closely and taken one alternative or the other. So far as I am personally concerned I am ready to take any alternative which this committee accepts, but we cannot accept both.

The commission was not a
commission of lawyers or draftsmen; it was a commission making certain recommendations which it was expected would be put into proper form by the draftsmen. The language of the recommendations was general and the language has been greatly changed. I do not say the change has been for the worse. The language used by the commission could not have been put in statutory form and it was not intended as such. I do not think it is correct for the minister to say that we should have drafted this at the time we made our report.
You should have decided as between statute law and common law. That is all that I am suggesting.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I confess that it has
been a matter of concern to me to know just how to cure the difficulties to which the hon. member and other hon. members have referred. I wonder if we said something about the shares not being sold at a discount, or fixed an amount which could not be exceeded, would we not meet some of the difficulties? The English statute in the terms in which the minister has just read it represents the statute as it was finally settled at the instance of Mr. Asquith. At that time difficulties arose in England in connection with the inadequate value of properties being turned over to companies for large numbers of shares, in the days of the great promotions. This resulted in a commission being appointed under the chairmanship of Mr. Frank Crisp, an eminent solicitor who was made a baronet for his services. He prepared the statute which was put through the English house, assisted by others. I recall very vividly the disoussion which took place as to how one might overcome the difficulties to which attention has been directed this afternoon. The different provincial legislatures have endeavoured to deal with this matter and I sent out and got a case which I recalled being before the supreme court. This was an Alberta case, and as the minister has said, the court had to draw a very clear distinction between those who were the original beneficiaries of the stock watering and those who acquired the shares for valuable consideration after they had been issued fully paid. That distinction has been carried through all the cases. When we get down to having a declaration of the consideration in cash or services or property I find it very difficult to accommodate my mind to the thought that those points are not so elastic as to permit of almost anything.
That is my difficulty. Should we do something in the way of deciding the discounts at which the shares should be issued, or providing that they could not be issued as fully paid up at a discount of more than so much? When I buy a share in a company I assume that one hundred cents in the dollar is being paid into the treasury, and when I discover that because of property or services which have been exchanged for shares, the shares have a value of only twenty-five cents on the dollar I find my investment rather bad. How are we going to cure this? I am curious to hear the amendment which has been suggested by Mr. Wegenast. I have been informed that when the Department of Justice
Companies Act Amendment

were considering these sections they gave considerable thought to them and the difficulty of arriving at any single conclusion was just as great then as it has been here this afternoon. We all would like to see this done, but how are we going to do it? Is there anything in the statute as it now stands in connection with the sale of shares at a discount? I confess that this afternoon my mind is not working sufficiently to remember that.

If its par value represents
one hundred cents on the dollar, nothing can be adequate as compensation for that share unless it is adequate to the extent of one hundred cents on the dollar. There is no doubt of that in my mind.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: And the test of that?

The test of that rests with the courts. We can go on and provide, as they have provided by section 47 of the English act, that it shall be lawful for a company to issue at a discount shares in the company of a class already issued. When you are first issuing shares having par value they must represent one hundred cents on the dollar of par value although there is no express provision in the 1929 English act to that effect.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: They overcome that by the provision in connection with the commission on sales.

In order to allow a company, the value of whose assets has depreciated, to secure new capital at a discount, section 47 of 'the English act provides that the issue of shares at a discount must be authorized by a resolution passed at a general meeting of the company and must be sanctioned !by the count in practically the same way as a compromise arrangement. The resolution must specify the maximum rate of discount at which shares are to be issued. But the English act assumes that when you so provide for a discount there must be compensation paid for the shares and in respect of shares with par value, that compensation must be the par value less the rate of discount. I have heard a suggestion to that effect made from time to time and if the hon. member for Kings-Hanfs wishes to move that amendment we will consider it.

This would not be an amendment to this section, it would be a new section. I move:
That the following section be inserted between sections 45 and 4-6 of the act:
45A. Every shareholder shall, until the whole of the par value or the issue price, as

the case may be, of his shares shall have been paid up, be liable to pay to the company or to its liquidator or to the trustee in bankruptcy of its estate any amount unpaid on such shares.

As the Prime Minister has pointed out, this section 45 is an important one and I think further consideration of the verbiage of the section would be justified. The Secretary of State has referred to the liability of a shareholder who is not an allottee.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: A purchaser for value without notice.

I am not sure that the case to which he referred would apply, as apparently by this section the whole transaction is made illegal. The section reads:
In no case shall any shares, whether common or preferred, or whether with or without nominal or par value, be issued and allotted as fully or partly paid' up for less than what may justly be deemed in all the circumstances of the case adequate consideration therefor-
Where a share was, contrary to this provision, wrongfully or illegally issued as fully paid up, that share might be tainted in the hands of anyone who might obtain it from then on.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is just what they held in the case from Alberta.

That is my fear there. This brings me to the point made by the Secretary of State. It may be possible that a time limit could be imposed such as that contained in section 41 of the English act. I think that section applies to the time limit within which an allottee of shares may revoke his allotment and reject his subscription on the grounds of fraud and misrepresentation. The same idea could be made apply here so that one who bought shares could feel that the bars were up and no action could be brought. Section 157 of the English act provides a time limit; anyone who has parted with his shares for one year is not longer liable. But I realize that that does not apply to the case in point.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The last English act.

That still leaves the present holder of the shares liable, if my theory is right, that he is holding shares illegally issued. Thirdly, with regard to what my hon. friend from Hants-Kings has said, with respect to the effect of Section 45, it is true it is only in terms a section which limits liability. I do not know whether it is correct to say it, but I have always had the idea that if a per-

Companies Act Amendment
son were a member of a company and the liability were not limited by statute he might be in the position of a partner and liable to the full extent of the liabilities of the company.
That is the law.

If that is the case you would not need a statute imposing liability, such as my hon. friend has suggested, because the fact that a person is a member of a company, whether his holding is to the extent of $4 or $4,000, makes him a partner and he is liable.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Recent authorities do not go quite so far. They pare down that theory and hold that the liability is limited by the value of the shares.
That may be.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There has been an effort to do that.

My hon. friend from Hants-Kings suggests that the theory is limited to companies incorporated by memorandum of association, because they are contractual as compared with charter companies incorporated under this act. I had the idea that if it were not for the fact that the provision of the statute limits liability, the liability would be unlimited. However, my hon. friend feels that he wants to go the other way about it and put in a positive section imposing liability. Section 157 of the English act does. I am not sure that we are talking by the book, because it may be that the Winding-up Act does it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The Winding-up Act defines the measure of liability but it does not make it unlimited. I am speaking from memory, but I do not think it does.

The English act imposes a positive liability on the shareholder, which my hon. friend says is not contained in section 45 as it stands. Coming back to section 5 again, I suggest to the Secretary of State that it would be worth while if he allowed the section to stand. May I refer however to subsection (10), which prohibits what have come to be known as management or control shares. I have received several representations with regard to this matter to the effect that there does not seem to be any point in making this subsection apply to what we know as private companies, that is, companies whose shares are not subscribed for by the public, the transfer of whose shares 92582-246
is restricted, and companies the number of whose shareholders is limited. I understand that there are companies owned largely by foreigners which pay some revenue to this country, composed of people who live outside Canada and who hold shares which represent the equity. They have another class of shares which control the management?

Would it not be sufficient to strike out, at the top of page 3, the word "the" in the first line, and to insert in place thereof "a public company," so as to read "in no case shall shares of a public company of any class"-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is the public company aimed at, because of difficulties that arose in consequence of financial control, I will not say by exploiters but by houses that took properties and dealt with them for the purpose of controlling them.
Groups.

Yesterday, the hon. -member for Bast Kootenay (Mr. Stevens), referring to myself, said:
The minister who introduced this legislation stated in one part of his remarks that if he were in private practice he would like nothing better than to be briefed to contest the very measures he was introducing.

I said I did not regard it as adequate to prevent shareholders, iby private arrangement, obtaining -control of a company and so control of the management of -the company. One of the things most to be desired is to obtain continuity of management, and in many public companies this is not obtained by management shares. I have never incorporated a company with management shares; but I have found several ways whereby, by consent and cooperation or by agreement on the part of a majority of the shareholders, continuity of management could be maintained. That is all I had in -mind at the time.

Mr. BOTHWEiLL: In this particular section, what exactly is the object of doing away with the deferred shares?

I do not know; I have no idea what was in the mind of the commission who recommended it. Perhaps the hon. member for Hants-Kings can inform us. Deferred shares, in practice, do not usually come into the first organization of a company, in my experience at any rate; but we have had during the past four years many compromises as between shareholders and creditors representing different interests in which eferred shares are authorized and my hon. friend knows that such compromise arrangements

are permitted under the act with the approval of the court. Under the supervision of a judge of the superior court of the province in which the head office of the company is, and in considering such compromise arrangements I have frequently found provisions that some of the ordinary shareholders should become deferred shareholders in order that a more equitable arrangement might be reached. I have not seen this in our Canadian practice except as arising out of such compromises.

I have been informed that this is a very useful manner of financing a company; that is, some shareholders, particularly in mining companies, are quite willing that dividends should be deferred to them until the company is in a position to pay the deferred dividends. I am not well enough versed in thie matter to be able to argue the point, and I shall leave it to others.

It apparently devolves upon me to justify this recommendation. In a general way I think the members of the price spreads commission felt there should be a simplification of share issues and the placing upon the market of a number of different classes of shares was confusing to the general public and led to people buying shares of a different class from the ones they felt they were buying. That, generally speaking, was what was in the minds of the commission. I am very doubtful whether our attention was specifically directed to deferred shares; I do not think it was. There was no intention to cut out deferred shares as such, but it was felt it was desirable not to have too many classes or types of shares. That is the basis of the recommendation.

I would suggest that we
pass the section as it stands and leave the question of deferred shares for future consideration or for another parliament because to change it now it going to lead to controversy.

I want to refer to section 96B which speaks of "adequate consideration in cash, property or services." Cash payments are always a tangible thing, and the same applies to property, but it is often hard to arrive at an accurate conclusion as to services. It is in that connection that most of the abuses have arisen in my section of the country, leaving mining aside altogether. I think it would not be beyond the power of this committee to establish a certain rate for services. The Secretary of State may not be aware of it, but in certain cases the services for the promotion of certain Companies are obtained on a cash paid basis and also on the basis of the actual value of the property.
I think the purposes of this bill will be defeated unless we find it possible to remedy that situation.
I do not think anyone in the country will quarrel with the principle of this bill as it is a step forward in the remedying of the evils of monopolies. Both the Secretary of State

and the committee are aware of the single liability of promoters in stock companies. This is one of the great causes of abuse in this country. The small store-keeper, the small mill owner or the small business man who is forced into bankruptcy may lose all his assets while the man who has invested his money in a limited stock company is responsible only for the amount he has paid in. We have a double liability provision in connection with shareholders in banks and I believe it would be a step in the right direction to provide that shareholders in stock companies shall have at least a double liability. This would be one of the best means of remedying the abuses of monopolies. The small store-keeper may lose even his personal belongings while the man who has invested in the limited company is responsible only for what he has paid in.
I notice the mining companies are not included and I believe this is due to certain provincial laws, more particularly the blue sky laws of Ontario. When those laws are carried out it is practically impossible to have anything but proper promotion of companies. I should like the Secretary of State to consider a more definite description of the services to be rendered and consider also the putting into effect of a double liability in connection with shareholders.

The house in committee on Bill No. 11, to amend the Interest Act-Mr. Coote-Mr. Smith (Cumberland) in the chair.
On section 1-Interest on contracts and agreements restricted to seven per cent.

Mr. Chairman, this Bill
No. 11 was originally introduced early in the session and it was some time before it was reported on by the committee. Only one of the sections, which is the important one of the bill as introduced, was in the bill as finally passed by the committee and reported to the house. The bill as introduced called for a limitation on the rate of interest on all mortgages, whether now existing or to be made in the future, to four per cent, but as amended in the committee that limitation would apply only to existing mortgages, and the cut-off date has been fixed in the bill as January 1, 1935. So the bill now before the house would

Interest Act Amendment
limit the rate of interest which -might be collected on any mortgage on real estate issued prior to January, 1935, to six per cent per annum. Speaking for myself I would be quite willing to have it apply to all mortgages, but in our own province so far as I am aware there are very feiw new mortgages being made.
The interest rate on existing mortgages is the important question for us, and I would just like to take a few minutes to bring to the attention of the committee a few facts to show that undoubtedly there is need of legislation to deal with this question of interest rates. I will deal first with the interest rate on farm mortgages.
The cash income of all the farms in Canada for the years 1926, 1927, 1928 and 1929, before the depression years, was 4,012 million dollars, and for the years 1931, 1932, 1933 and 1934, that is the depression years, the cash income of all the farms in Canada was 1,744 million dollars, or only 43 per cent in those last four years of the income in the previous four years mentioned. In other words, there was a drop in the last four years of 2,268 million dollars in farm income or an average of over 550 million dollars for each one of those years. In the -face of that drop in revenue, which amounts on -the average for the four years to $3,136 per farm, I think hon. members can see the need for some legislation to relieve the farmers who are now -paying rates of interest as high as seven, eight and nine per cent. This drop in income per farm of $3,136 in the last four years would have been sufficient to pay off every farmer's debt in Canada and leave about $1,000 for every farm over and above the amount of the debt.
The drop in farm revenue is, of course, due to the drop in price levels. It is not due, as some people may think, to a drop in production. I have previously put figures on Hansard to show that it is nearly all due to the drop in price levels, a factor over which the farmer himself had no control and n-o possibility of control.
The rate at present charged in western Canada, at least in Alberta, is generally eight per cent, although there are some mortgages at nine per cent. A case recently came before the board of review operating under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act in the province of Alberta of a real estate mortgage carrying a rate of interest of twenty per cent. I have that statement in a letter from one of the members of the board of review. There are also a good -many private loans at ten per cent. I do not think it is necessary for me
to say anything more for hon. members of this committee to see the need of some legislation -to limit the rate of interest which can be collected on these mortgages.
The board of review under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act in Alberta have in the majority of instances been setting the rate of interest on farm mortgages by mortgage companies at seven per cent, which I think is much too high, but the chairman of the board persists in stating, I believe, that it is the duty of parliament to set a lower rate. The rate of seven per cent is mentioned in one of the sections of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. In Manitoba I believe the board in the last few weeks has been setting a maximum rate of six per cent on farm mortgages. In Quebec I am told that in some cases the rate on farm mortgages has been placed as low as four per cent by the board of review operating in that province.
The Alberta board has heard about three hundred cases to date. It has been sitting five days a week and working very hard, but it is going to take them some yea-rs to clear up all the cases that come before them unless something is done to fix by law a -maximum rate of interest. I think this bill is fixing the rate quite high enough when it sets it at six per cent. If a six per cent maximum rate were established by law I believe that the majority of farmers in the province of Alberta would not need to go to the board of review. The only way to get a lower rate of interest -than eight per cent in Alberta is to go before the board of review, and if the board of review establishes as a matter of practice a rate of seven per cent the mortgage companies naturally will not care to make a voluntary reduction to anything lower -than seven per cent.
I want to place on Hansard for the benefit of this committee a statement in regard to the payments made by one farmer at Brant, Alberta. I mentioned this case in the banking committee, where the figures were challenged by several members. They said they could not possibly be correct. I afterwards wrote to the chairman of the banking committee and asked him to have the -clerk or someone else inquire into the case. The books of the company that made the loan were examined and I have here a copy of the memorandum which was sent to the finance minister by Mr. Finlayson, the superintendent of insurance, who investigated the case. I shall not take time to put the whole of his statement on Hansard, but will simply say that the loan was made in February, 1912, for $1,500 at a rate
Interest Act Amendment

of eight per cent. By 1928, according to this statement, the farmer had paid $3,587.28, and $708 of that amount was subsequently paid out by the company for taxes, so that the net amount which the farmer paid was $2,878.32. This was all for interest and charges, including fire insurance, $61.50; inspection fee, $37.50; solicitors' fees, $57.03. In 1933 this mortgage was foreclosed. I am quoting these figures simply for the purpose of impressing on the committee just how much money it would require from the farmers' operations to meet these charges. Over a period Of twenty years he paid $2,878, and when the loan was foreclosed the amount that he still owed was approximately $1,500. If we could have had in Canada a six per cent interest rate, and the other two per cent which was charged could have been used to amortize the loan, it would have been entirely paid off and the farmer would still be in possession of his farm.
Just a word or two in regard to urban mortgages. I have had brought to my attention the case of a mortgage on a house in the city of Calgary at the rate of ten per cent, and I have a letter under my hand from a notary in one of the cities of Ontario in which he says:
I can number mortgagors among my clients, whose total indebtedness is well over $100,000, upon which they are paying from eight per cent to ten per cent interest.
As an alderman of the city I am pleased at the thought that our tax arrears will be paid up now that interest charges on properties are reduced.
That is from an alderman in an Ontario city. He is a little premature in thinking that the interest charges are already reduced. I had a visit a few days ago from some gentlemen representing the landlords' protective association of Montreal and they assured me that there are many real estate mortgages in that city which bear interest rates of seven and eight per cent and second mortgages bearing interest rates of nine and ten per cent. In some cases the mortgage may show upon its face only a rate of seven or eight per cent but a very heavy discount is sometimes made when the loan is granted. An alderman in one city in Canada told me that he believed in certain -cases the rate actually collected was as high as twenty per cent, taking into account the discounts made when the loan was granted.
I anticipate that the question of constitutionality will be raised, that it will be stated that the Dominion of Canada has not the power to lower the rate of interest on exist-

ing obligations, but if I remember correctly, a year or two ago the attorneys general of the provinces agreed that this power rested in the dominion government. In these days when the government is passing reform measures which heretofore might have been considered as unconstitutional I do not think we would be running much risk in passing this bill. The only way in which to find out whether it is constitutional is to try it.
I anticipate also that some question will be raised as to this action affecting our credit in outside countries, particularly Great Britain. I would remind the committee that Great Britain recently notified the United States that she did not intend to make certain payments which were due about this time. I think for the last two or three years Great Britain has been making token payments. The United States itself changed the terms of the contract when they stated that a promise to pay in gold need not be honoured in the term in which it was taken, that payment in legal tender or paper currency will be sufficient to discharge the debt. I shall not labour this point; it has been discussed before.
I would remind the committee that nearly every country in the world has taken some action along the lines which I suggest in this bill. Australia, South Africa, I believe New Zealand, and many other countries have taken action to limit the rates of interest which can be collected regardless of what might be stated in the mortgages. When I offered an amendment to the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act to limit the rates of interest charged on farm mortgages, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) said that the proper way to deal with that matter would be through Bill No. 11. He said:
My hon. friend speaks for the farmer who is not going to come under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. That farmer will get such protection as this house may decide to accord him when it deals with Bill No. 11, which covers all mortgages.
According to that statement this will be the only occasion upon which we will have an opportunity to deal with this very important question.
There is a crying need for this bill; I would not have introduced it had I not felt there was such a need. The fall in price levels which I mentioned earlier in my remarks is something over which the farmer had no control. He had no reason to anticipate such a fall and he entered into his obligations in good faith. In the great majority of cases the farmers are doing their best to discharge their

Franchise Act Amendment
obligations. The company or individual collecting eight or nine per cent in interest charges is receiving a purchasing power far in excess of what was anticipated. It would be nothing less than justice to reduce the rate of interest to six per cent; even at that rate the majority of mortgages would secure in purchasing power just as much as they did ten years ago when the mortgages were made. For this and many other reasons I hope that the committee will see fit to accept this bill. I know it is near the end of the session but I introduced the bill early in the session but for some weeks I could not. get the banking committee to meet.
