subtopic: EVIDENCE IN APPEAL, TO JUDGE FROM RULING OF REGISTRAR OF ELECTORS
speechtext:
With regard to the amendment suggested by the hon. member for Shelbume-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston), 1 would remind the house that this bill is simply a declaratory act; it declares the intention of the house with respect to the meaning and intent of the subsection referred to. This bill was introduced at the suggestion of the Dominion franchise commissioner and was approved by him. He did not approve of it because it related to the electoral list in
the electoral district which I have the honour to represent, but, unless the bill is carried into effect, he fears that as a result a very considerable number of appeals throughout Canada will be taken to the judges having jurisdiction in the several constiuencies. This bill is in entire accord with his understanding of the meaning and intent of the sections now proposed to be amended. The bill is entirely consistent and conforms with the instructions he has given to each registrar of electors throughout the dominion. From one end of the country to the other, in respect of each electoral district, the registrars have acted in accordance with his instructions in carrying out the real intent and purpose of the act as expressed in this bill. Therefore, if utter confusion is to be avoided, he thinks the house should make this declaration.
Perhaps the other day I referred at too great length to what had occurred in my own constituency, but I do say here that so far as the registrar acted in that electoral district he acted under the specific instructions of the dominion franchise commissioner, who is the sole person under the act entitled to give him instructions. It is not necessary for me to add that so far as the commissioner gave his instructions under section 7 of the existing act he did so without consulting me as the minister to whom he reports; and, so far as the registrar in the electoral district of St. Lawrence-St. George carried out those instructions, he carried them out without communication with me directly or indirectly, because I have had no personal communication with him from the day he was appointed up to the present time-and he was appointed, as all registrars were appointed, many months ago. The government therefore is of opinion under the circumstances that to avoid confusion throughout the whole country it cannot accept the amendment suggested by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth.

subtopic: EVIDENCE IN APPEAL, TO JUDGE FROM RULING OF REGISTRAR OF ELECTORS
speechtext:
I have listened with great care to the remarks made by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan); I also listened to the debate that took place in this house some days ago regarding this bill, and as well to the statements made by the hon. member who has taken his seat, with reference to the fact that this is only a declaratory bill. The house will remember that when the bill was introduced the hon. gentleman, in introducing it, discussed a judgment of Mr. Justice Greenshields, who gave a decision in this matter. We have heard differences of opinion expressed by the hon. gentleman with respect to the contents
Franchise Act Amendment

of that judgment in relation to the provisions and the regulations under the act. In justice to the judge who rendered judgment in this matter and who cannot defend himself, who gave judgment in accordance with the provisions of the law; and in view of the high office he occupies in the country at the present time and the fact that before he went to the bench he was one of the most eminent jurists of our province and one of the leading legal lights of the country, being still considered one of the best judges on our judiciary, I think it is only fair for me to say a few words with reference to the grounds on which the learned judge based his judgment and the considerations which he indicated in coming to his conclusion. I think it is only proper that I should discuss the matter from that point of view in order to find out whether we are justified now in proceeding with this bill which the hon. gentleman has introduced.
I have in my hand what purports to be a copy of the judgment rendered on the 4th day of June in the city of Montreal in this very matter:
Province of Quebec.
District of Montreal.
Superior Court
Under The Dominion Franchise Act Electoral Division St. Lawrence and St. George
Daniel McKeegan
Appellant
and
Rudolph Bernard Registrar & Revising Officer and
W. K. Prowse
Objector
This is an appeal from the ruling or order of the registrar under section 32 of the Dominion Franchise Act. That section provides, in part, as follows:
I will leave out section 32, which refers to the right of appeal and is contained in the act. The judgment proceeds:
On the 22nd of May, 1935, the registrar and revising officer. Mr. Rudolph Bernard, struck from the official list of electors the names of two hundred persons appearing on the regular official list of voters for the electoral division of St. Lawrence and St. George, and particularly on polls Nos. 17, 18, 19 and 31. These names all appeared in the notice of appeal entered by Daniel McKeegan, a duly qualified elector of the electoral division of St. Lawrence and St. George.
The names of these electors were so struck from the official list of voters upon an objection made to them by one, W. R. Prowse.
With the exception of the statement concerning a few of the two hundred, the unique and sole objection was, that they had removed from the electoral division, or at least, the poll in which their names were entered.

It may be here stated, that after the notice of appeal was served on the registrar, the objector, Prowse, desisted from his objection, and purported to desist from the order given by the registrar striking the names of twenty-three out of the two hundred. The registrar decided that notwithstanding the withdrawal of the objection by the objector, and the declaration of his willingness to desist from the order striking the electors' names, he was unable to replace their names on the list. The appeal with respect to these twenty-three must be maintained, and acte is granted of the objector's declaration that he withdraws his objection, and the order goes to the registrar, to place these names on the voters' list as they appeared before the order of striking, and in the respective polls in which they appeared.
With respect to the remaining one hundred and' seventy-seven, I now proceed to consider their appeals.
The names objected to all appeared on the official voters' list before the registrar or revising officer. Each one is entitled to exercise the franchise and is entitled to vote, unless and until it is affirmatively shown, either that he never possessed that right, or that he has forfeited the right. In other words, the presumption of law is, that each one of these electors is properly and legally on the list of voters, and in consequence, is entitled to exercise his franchise. The rule of law is expressed in the Roman maxim: "Omnia prae-sum-unter rite et solleniter esse acta."
The objector seeks to destroy the right of these electors to exercise the franchise, on the ground that they hqve lost their right by reason of a change of residence or domicile. Section 28 of the act deals with the proceedings before the revision court:
I will not put on the record this section, which is the procedure of the registrar and the revisal courts. The judge then goes on:
I propose to deal with these appeals in the light of and under the provisions of this section, and I observe, firstly, that the registrar must deal with each objection separately, and he must deal with the merits of the objection as disclosed by the examination under oath of the objector, and the person against whom the objection is made, always provided, I take it, that both are present.	I next observe that the person
against whom an objection is made, and who has received a notice under section 21, is not bound to attend, and his failure to attend does not relieve the objector from substantiating the existence of the fact upon which his objection is based. Moreover, the presumption in favour of the person against whom the objection is made is recognized in the statute. Such elector is under no obligation to adduce proof that his name is properly on the list. Again, it must be observed, and even emphasized, that the objector must offer proof substantiating a prima facie case by evidence, which, in the absence of rebuttal, is considered by the registrar sufficient to establish the fact, not a presumption, but the actual fact, that the person objected to is improperly on the list.
I now deal with the proceedings before the registrar, on the twenty-second of May, as disclosed before me. In the first place Prowse

Franchise Act Amendment
was the objector in all the two hundred cases. From his own testimony it appears that he did not know, personally, one of the two hundred against whom he made an objection. In the second place, he never saw one of these electors against whom he made these objections. What he did appears by his testimony. He went to the residence, as shown on the official voters' list. In some cases he found a vacant house, or a house into which he could not obtain entrance. How long that house had been vacant he has no idea. He therefore asked somebody for information, and' somebody, whom he had never seen before, and whom he does not know, informed him, that the house was vacant: that the former tenant had moved away. This statement covers a comparatively few of the names objected to. In the great majority of the names the objector Prowse, found someone in the house. Again, he did not know that person, but asked that person if the elector lived there, and was told by that person, no, and Prowse testified to what	he	had heard before	the registrar.He was	never asked	for	the	name of hisinformant, and if he had, he could not have given the name. At the hearing of the appeal I expressed the opinion, that this in itself was not prima facie evidence sufficient to establish the fact that the name of the person objected	to	was, to	use	the	words of thestatute, improperly on the list. In other words, it was not prima facie evidence that the elector	objected	to	was	no longer a
resident within the limits of the polling division in which his name appeared. But the registrar says that registered letters sent by him to each of the persons whose names are objected to. were returned and were not delivered. Why. he does not know, and no one, so far as the record shows, can tell it.
In addition to this, a lady by the name of Ruth Clark obtained information from someone that an elector, whose name appears on poll No. 17 no longer resided at a certain number. How she discovered that is not disclosed. But she concludes by the statement, that she is credibly informed and verily believes, that the elector is no longer a qualified elector.
These affidavits I may state at once, the registrar admits, he never read. They never should have been read by him, and, as a matter of fact, they are not part of the proof made before the registrar. The registrar did state that he had read one perhaps of the two hundred, but he does admit that his ruling was not based upon these affidavits. The section of the act does not contemplate the making of proof before the registrar by ex parte affidavits. The act is silent on the matter of the use of affidavits. The act contemplates proof being made before the registrar by witnesses. Says the act:
"The registrar shall deal with each objection separately disclosed by examination on oath of the person making the objection, the person against whom the objection is made and the witnesses present on their respective behalf." It does not contemplate the production of affidavits purporting to support or substantiate the statement of fact made by the objector without any opportunity of the signers of the affidavit to be cross-examined as to their truth by the person against whom they are sought to be used.
I conclude that the registrar had not a scintilla of legal proof to make even a prima 92582-247
facie case, much less to establish the fact that any of these two hundred electors were improperly on the list and should be struck therefrom.
It was urged that one or two of the two hundred was dead. Fortunately for the dead person, there is no proof of death, and so far as the registrar is concerned and the proof made he is alive. I maintain the appeal in all the two hundred cases, and I order and direct the registrar to replace their names upon the official voters' list at the different polls in the electoral division of St. Lawrence and St. George as they appeared before being struck therefrom.
R. A. E. Greenshields,

We have before the committee at the present time the fact upon which is based the act and the amendment to the act that we are now considering. Mr. Justice Greenshields based his decision upon the sections of the act just quoted and upon the evidence that was adduced before him. When I heard the other day the hon. member who is sponsoring the bill state that no evidence was made before Mr. Justice Greenshields, as regards the kind of statements signed before witnesses that he was talking about as evidence, there is no proof that such statements were submitted to Mr. Justice Greenshields. He had to revise the decision of the registrar in this ease. If we look at the evidence that was given at a certain time before Mr. Justice Greenshields, we find that he decided this case on its very merits; and also by the evidence that was adduced before the registrar, in some instances by questions that were put, and by the way he directed the evidence to be given, the proof is there that he acted within the meaning of the act and in order to try as far as possible to give justice to all parties concerned.
For instance, at page 42 of the examination of Mr. Bernard, the registrar, the court asks this question:
Q. I suppose he did not tell you from whom he had obtained the information?
The answer is:
From somebody, some neighbour. In the case where the house was vacant, or the tenement was vacant, from the neighbour, and sometimes from the janitor.
By the court:
Q. In other words, all the information or assistance you got from Mr. Doyle-
Mr. Doyle was supposed to be a witness produced to corroborate what Mr. Prowse had stated.

was, from what somebody told him, and he offered you what somebody told him, is that it?
A. Yes, sir, in most cases.

Franchise Act Amendment

By the court:
Q. And it is true of Prowse, and it is true of Doyle?
A. Yes, sir.
By Mr. Manni:
Who was representing the interests of the hon. member who is sponsoring this bill.
Q. Let us see how true it is of Doyle. Is it not a fact that in many cases Doyle got the information direct from the person whose name was on the voters' list? Was not that evidence produced before you?
A. It is possible. I don't remember offhand.
By the court:
Q. Tell me now of one where that is true, and I will maintain your striking-tell me one elector who told Doyle that he had moved. Can you remember one of the two hundred?
A. I cannot at the present.

Mr. Bernard. I have before me the whole evidence. I would not like to weary the committee by putting into the record all the answers that were given by the witnesses that were produced before the registrar. Mr. Bernard and Mr. Prowse were the two witnesses who appear to have been cross-examined at length by counsel on both sides. I intend to place before the committee more particularly the part of the evidence which shows exactly what kind of evidence Mr. Justice Greenshields wanted to have, and which I think he was entitled in law and in equity to have before he could strike these names from the list. He inquired from the registrar if such evidence had been adduced and presented, and the registrar admitted that it had not. It is also shown in the proceedings that the registrar stated that in some cases the letter that was sent by registered mail was returned, but the judge stated that this was not prima facie proof that the person was not there. Everyone knows that a registered letter can be sent to an address, and if it is not signed for by the person receiving it at that house no one can say that the person duly received the [DOT] letter. I remember a recent case dealt with by the court of king's bench in the province of Quebec, in which I happened to be representing certain interested parties. It was the case of O'Shea and Michel, decided April 30, 1935. That case was decided on that very point; a registered letter had been sent but direct proof had not been produced that a receipt had been signed showing that the letter had been received by him, and the case was lost on that very ground. Apparently there is a method provided by the Post Office Department-and the Postmaster General might correct me if I am wrong-by which you may secure a proper certificate 
that a registered letter reached the person for whom it was intended. You pay an extra amount of some twenty or twenty-five cents and the person who receives the letter is bound to acknowledge receipt under his own signature. In these cases the only fact that appeared to have been proved was that registered letters had been sent, but the letters had been returned.
The other day the hon. gentleman stated that the registrar had been very diligent and had been very observant of the law in doing what had been done in putting into force the franchise act. I have no fault to find with this gentleman in the discharge of his duties. I happen to know Mr. Bernard very well; he is a member of the legal profession. I should like to place on record, however, a letter issued by the franchise commissioner, Colonel John Thompson, with reference to this matter, in which he gave to persons who were inquiring from him the following information:
May 21, 1935.
Thomas G. Ireland, Esq.,
Treasurer,
Liberal Association of St. Lawrence &
St. George,
252 Dorchester West,
Montreal Que.
Dear Sir:
Receipt is herewith acknowledged of your communication of the eighteenth instant, the contents of which have been carefully noted, and I quite concur in your observations.
The word "removal" in the statute does not mean the removal from one polling division to another in ' the same electoral district. "Removal" means removal from one electoral district to another.
While any person, during the month of April, might object to any and all persons on the list of an electoral district, nevertheless the objector must prove to the satisfaction of the registrar that the person or persons objected to have removed from the electoral district in which they are registered, to another electoral district.
The mere fact a person has left the dwelling in which he was originally registered does not in itself warrant the deletion of his name from the list of electors for that electoral district. The objector, as stated above, must prove that the person objected to has left the electoral district.
If an elector has moved from one polling division to another in the same electoral district, the proper procedure is to delete his name from the list of the polling division wherein he did reside and add it to the list he is presently residing.
Then the last paragraph:
The failure of the person objected to to appear at the court of revision in response to the registered notice of objection is not in itself sufficient to shift the onus for proving his entitlement on the person objected to.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd.) John Thompson, Dominion Franchise Commissioner.

Franchise Act Amendment
So here we have a document emanating from the dominion franchise commissioner, who is in charge of the act that was passed last year, giving information as to the manner in which these proceedings should be carried out. That information, it seems to me, is not quite consistent with the objections that have been taken by those supporting the bill now under consideration, who have taken exception to the rulings handed down by Mr. Justice Greenshields in the superior court of the province of Quebec.
During the course of the debate the other day the hon. gentleman who is sponsoring this bill stated that Mr. Bernard had done his best to administer the law fairly and within the provisions of the act. I do not know if my information is correct; I give it subject to correction, but I hold in my hand a copy of the instructions issued by the franchise commissioner, and at page 86 I find the following:

He asked the registrar if he had documents and records before him, and the registrar said that he did not keep any. Now, Mr. Chairman, we have this most unfortunate situation to-day. The franchise act has been administered by the franchise commissioner, who is highly qualified to administer the act and for whom everybody in this house and in the country has nothing but praise. But it develops that in only one constituency, the constituency of St. Law-rence-St. George, there was apparently some trouble in the revision of the list, because we have heard of no trouble at all in any other part of Canada. It may be that my learned friend is very cautious and his men want to make very sure that he will be reelected next time, and the people there who look after the whole matter for him worked so hard that they thought they would have a case against everybody on the list who they thought would vote against the hon. member, to see that they were not on the list.

I did not say the hon. member himself did it. I said that those who were looking after his election were doing so much work for him that they did not want the fruits of their work thrown away, and they were mad when they were not able to get what they wanted. We are not sitting here in this House of Commons, Mr. Chairman, as a court of review over any judgment that has been given in accordance with the provisions of any act passed by this parliament. We decided rightly or wrongly that the chief justice of any province should be the sole

arbiter and sole judge of any difficulty that might arise in any proceedings beware the registrar regarding the striking off or putting on of names. But to-day we have this most unfortunate situation. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George says that there are four thousand objections in his constituency and that at the present time only two hundred of them have been dealt with. Twenty-three were not in doubt and the rest, 177, had to be dealt with by the judge. At the present time there are many other cases in this very constituency of St. Lawrence-St. George that depend on the decision that is to be rendered by this parliament by this bill if it becomes law.
I was very much struck the other day by the observations that were made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) when dealing with conditions which affect the judiciary in our country. The very next day after the Secretary of State had introduced this bill, he received this condemnation at the hands of his leader. The Prime Minister, speaking in this house on June 19, 1935, as reported on page 3810 of Hansard, was saying that we should respect the judgments of the privy council, and that therefore we could not go too far in this new order and with these new reforms that the government was bringing in. These were his words:
That is why I have said that in the ultimate analysis we always have to depend upon the conclusions and decisions of the courts. That is why in the end, if we are a law abiding people who believe in reform and not in revolution, we must proceed precept by precept, line upon line, to the end that in an orderly and legal manner we may accomplish the ends we have in mind.
Here we have a condemnation by the leader of the government of the proceedings of the Secretary of State in introducing his bill, which strikes at the very root of our judicial institutions. Again, speaking in this house on June 20, 1935, the Prime Minister said, as reported at pages 3820 and 3821 of Hansard- he was referring to the capital structure of the Canadian National Railways:
I desire on that ground to make it clear why I do not desire until this litigation is disposed of any disturbance in the capital structure.
He was referring to the capital structure of the Canadian National Railways and he wanted us to refrain from doing anything while the litigation was before the privy council. Certain matters have been dealt with in accordance with the legislation enacted last year and because Chief Justice

Marketing Act-Mr. Weir (Meljort)
Greensliields has decided contrary to the wishes of friends of the hon. gentleman we are being asked to remedy this supposed grievance. I think if we did that we would be going beyond the powers of this parliament; we would 'be undermining our institutions and our judiciary. We would be going against the courts for which the right hon. gentleman who leads the government has so much respect. I think the hon. gentleman, should have remembered that when a judgment is rendered there is always forty-eight hours in which to criticize or, if I may use the expression, damn the judge. He should have let it go at that; he should have remained quiet and taken his licking in good humour. That is the only way in which the hon. gentleman should have acted.
When one has a following in a riding it is very difficult not to yield to their demands and requests. Should this bill pass, the hands of the judge would be tied and he would not be able to render a decision as the law now provides it should be rendered. If this bill is passed the general effect will be that the chief justice will be deprived of the right to comment upon the evidence which the registrar has accepted as sufficient. If this bill becomes law we may have every reason to expect that after June 29 the registrar will again adopt his old practice and will strike off the names of a large number of electors upon grounds which the chief justice has already declared to be insufficient. This action will be taken without any possible means of redress by the electors concerned.
This bill is obviously designed to meet a case which has arisen in the particular riding represented by the hon. member for St. Law-rence-St. George. In this riding the names Objected to number 4,000 while the total number of electors is about 24,000. If the hon. gentleman and his friends have their way, one-sixth of the electors in this constituency will be disqualified from voting. I think in this case we would do well to follow the example set by the right hon. gentleman in his speeches of June 19 and 20 when he said that it would be better to abide by the conclusions and decisions of the court. He said that we should leave the matter at that because that was the only way in which we could obtain and accomplish what we had in mind in an ordinary and legal manner.
I think the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) should be accepted, as it makes it clear that the legislation sponsored by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George
would not affect the present cases which are awaiting the decision of Chief Justice Green-shields.
